title: Merge Sort, LeetCode, and Why I Still Think This Stuff Is Cool
description: A casual breakdown of a LeetCode problem and how it led into rethinking merge sort from scratch in Rust.

content.text: The Two Sneaky Numbers of Digitville is a LeetCode easy. The problem basically asks you to find two numbers in an array that appear twice.

For example: [0, 1, 1, 0]. The numbers 0 and 1 both appear twice. It’s an easy problem for a reason — you could probably come up with a solution without even really knowing much about computer science.

I wasn’t really trying to grind LeetCode or anything, I just wanted something fun to pass the time. But while working on it, I ended up thinking about merge sort again, which honestly reminded me why I like it in the first place.
So this turned into me just writing down my thought process and the version of merge sort I ended up using.
My Relationship with Merge Sort

When I code, I usually try to stick with simplicity. I don’t like jumping straight to solutions that feel like they come from someone way above my skill level. Not because they’re bad, but because I don’t actually learn anything that way.

And yeah — this is also where I kind of struggle with LeetCode (and honestly AI-assisted coding too). It’s really easy to just copy a solution and move on, but then you don’t actually understand what’s happening.
Anyway, merge sort was one of those algorithms that clicked for me at some point, and I still think it’s kind of beautiful.
A Simple Mental Model of Merge Sort
At its core, merge sort is a depth-first algorithm. You recursively split an array until every sub-array has just one element. At that point, everything is trivially sorted.
Then you start merging those small arrays back together in sorted order.
The part that always gets skipped over in explanations is the merge step itself — but that’s actually where most of the logic lives.
The Merge Step (The Important Part)
The merge function is actually pretty simple. You keep two pointers, one for each array, and repeatedly take the smaller value.

So if we take two arrays like:
[left] = [0, 2]
[right] = [1, 2]
The merge process looks like this:

Compare 0 and 1 → take 0
merged = [0]

Compare 2 and 1 → take 1
merged = [0, 1]

Compare 2 and 2 → take either
merged = [0, 1, 2]
What About the Remaining Elements?
The loop stops when one array runs out, but you still need to handle whatever is left in the other array.
This works because the leftover elements are already sorted. That’s the key idea people usually miss at first.
So Why Doesn’t This Break?
A few natural questions come up here:

1. What if one side finishes early?
2. What if the input arrays aren’t sorted?
3. Why does this actually improve performance?
The answer to (1) is exactly what those leftover loops handle — you just append the remaining elements.
For (2), yes — merge assumes both inputs are already sorted. But that’s where the recursion comes in.

Once you reach single elements, those are already sorted by definition.

So the reason merge sort works is because it never merges unsorted arrays. It only ever merges arrays that were already sorted at a smaller scale.
Final Thoughts
I think the most confusing part of merge sort isn’t the recursion — it’s the merge step itself and understanding why it works at all.
Once that clicks, the rest of it becomes way more intuitive. I think it feels elegant and its probably my favorite sorting algorithm.

The first time I learned it I thought it was so complicated but now Its one of the simplest sorting algorithms I know.
